output.brief: The gap is mostly a time-in-level effect, not a location effect. Only 32% of remote staff had the 18 months in level that the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. That is because remote hiring opened widely in July 2024, and 215 of the 340 remote staff started after March 2025. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28% vs 29%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and promotion rates (20% vs 21%) are nearly the same. The remote shortfall among eligible staff is about 1 point, and it rests on only 110 people, so a small real difference can't be ruled out. Remote staff don't leave more often than office staff (10.9% vs 11.6%). Remote staff are not concentrated in low-promotion job families. Don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would penalise people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misleading comparison. Do this instead: hold the proposal, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Some manager comments suggest remote staff get less visible work, but we have no data on that, so look at staffing records next. Confidence is fairly high on the main finding.
